newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl not to be rushed on new candidacy, aides say.
newsitem.headline: Kohl not to be rushed on new candidacy, aides say.

text.p: As pressure continued to mount on German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to say whether he will stand in next year's general election, top party sources said on Thursday a decision was not likely soon.
While Kohl kept his party and the country guessing, his most likely potential successor, Wolfgang Schaeuble, staked his claim as the helmsman to pilot through a bold reform programme.
Until this year, Kohl was widely seen as the best guarantee of returning the centre-right coalition of his Christian Democrats (CDU) and centrist Free Democrats (FDP) to power in October 1998.

But his failure to steer far-reaching tax and pension reform plans smoothly through the coalition, added to the blow of soaring unemployment, has unleashed ferment in the CDU and headlines of "Autumn of the Patriarch".

Kohl's indecision over whether to stand again has added to a sense of drift. But the party sources, who declined to be named, said his behaviour and comments suggested he would make a decision only after producing policy successes.
Kohl says he will ponder the matter after June's European Union reform summit, and the sources said progress on tax and pensions reform could by then provide a better backdrop for a new candidacy.

To decide now "would not solve a single current problem," one Kohl aide told Reuters. But even the conservative daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung urged the famously adept master of the power game not to look like a ditherer.
"Kohl is no longer the unchallenged master of what happens. If he doesn't want the twilight of the chancellor to become a polar night, he must make up his mind on 1998 soon."
If Kohl's star is dimming after nearly 15 years as chancellor, Schaeuble's is certainly rising.

Schaeuble, his ambition not dampened by an knife attack that left him paralysed from the waist down, reopened one of the rows which have shaken Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). He unceremoniously dismissed the pension plan of Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, darling of the party left.
In an interview in the weekly Wirtschaftswoche, the CDU parliamentary leader virtually accused proponents of Bluem's pensions reform of pork-barrel politics.
"I don't believe you can achieve the innovations we need in Germany through cowardice and opportunism," he said, dismissing Bluem's idea of raising tax to spread the pension fund's burden.

His comments caught a growing mood in the CDU that the reforms, touted as the bold step to carry the coalition through the next election, have hit such problems that only an iron hand can push them through -- if not Kohl's, then someone else's.

Four of the CDU's "wild bunch", the regional leaders aged about 40 who are becoming increasingly vocal and restive about their own futures, loyally told the weekly Die Woche they wanted Kohl to stand again -- but then lavished praise on Schaeuble.
"Schaeuble certainly has what it takes to be chancellor, and stands for strong leadership," said Ole van Beust, CDU leader in the Hamburg state assembly.
Schaeuble, 54, stole a march on rivals last month, almost certainly with Kohl's blessing, when he said he would probably not resist an opportunity to be chancellor.
That interview in the illustrated weekly Stern was part of a steady campaign to make his austere personality and above all his disability less forbidding to the German people.

Schaeuble's central role in negotiating the German unification treaty as interior minister in 1990 marked him out as Kohl's crown prince until a knife attack by a madwoman a week later left him paralysed and appeared to end his prospects.
But Schaeuble, now confined to a wheelchair, forced his way back into the political reckoning with more determination than ever.

His frank comments to Stern about what it felt like to be paralysed -- and an acknowledgement that people were entitled to ask whether Germany could be led by a disabled chancellor -- have set out to dismantle what he himself calls the "cripple taboo".
As yet, however, no one is suggesting Kohl's trusty lieutenant would try to oust the chancellor against his will.
